title: Matching: Maximal, Maximum, Perfect and Augmenting Paths
quickIdea: A matching pairs vertices through disjoint edges; maximal and maximum are different words, and flipping one augmenting path is the entire proof that a matching is not the largest.
remember: A matching M is a set of edges no two of which share a vertex, and a vertex is saturated by M when it is an endpoint of an edge of M.
Maximal means no edge can be added to M; maximum means no matching is larger. Every maximum matching is maximal, and a maximal matching can be half the size of the maximum.
Berge's theorem: M is maximum exactly when there is no M-augmenting path, meaning a path that alternates outside and inside M and starts and ends at unsaturated vertices.
Flipping an augmenting path, that is taking the symmetric difference with it, raises the size of the matching by exactly 1, which is the augmenting-path algorithm.
A perfect matching saturates every vertex, so n must be even; in a bipartite graph it also needs the two sides to be equal.
The number of matchings of a path on n vertices is the Fibonacci number F(n+1): 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34 for n = 1 to 8.
Every maximal matching has at least half as many edges as a maximum matching, since each matching edge can block at most two edges of the larger one.

example.prompt: How many matchings does a path on 8 vertices have?
example.work: Let M(n) be the count for a path on n vertices, with M(0) = M(1) = 1. Either the last edge is unused, giving M(n-1) matchings, or it is used, which forbids the edge before it and leaves M(n-2). So M(n) = M(n-1) + M(n-2), giving 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34.
example.answer: 34, which is F(9), and the empty matching is counted.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2026 Set 1 Q.47 asked this count as a NAT. Older papers ask 'maximal but not maximum' on a drawn graph. The recurrence and the two definitions are the whole question.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: How many perfect matchings does K_{n,n} have?
variations.answer: n factorial: assign the n left vertices to the n right vertices in every possible order.
variations.why: Every bijection between the two sides is exactly one perfect matching, and each pair of matched vertices has an edge in K_{n,n}.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: A matching M has 2 edges in a graph whose maximum matching has 3 edges. What must exist?
variations.answer: An M-augmenting path, by Berge's theorem.
variations.why: If no augmenting path existed, M would already be maximum, contradicting the larger matching.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: How many matchings does a cycle on 5 vertices have?
variations.answer: 11: the empty matching, 5 single edges, and 5 pairs of non-adjacent edges.
variations.why: Of the C(5,2) = 10 pairs of edges, the 5 adjacent pairs are not matchings, leaving 5 valid pairs.

trap.what: Treating 'maximal' as 'maximum', and forgetting that the empty set is a matching in counting questions.
trap.why: Maximal is a local statement about one matching; a larger matching can sit elsewhere in the same graph. And a matching need not contain any edge, which shifts every count by one.
trap.counterexample: On the path a-b-c-d the single edge bc is maximal, since every other edge shares b or c, yet the maximum matching {ab, cd} has 2 edges.

check.question: How many matchings does a path on 5 vertices have, and what is its maximum matching size?
check.answer: 8 matchings, which is F(6), and the maximum matching size is 2.
check.explanation: The recurrence gives M(5) = M(4) + M(3) = 5 + 3 = 8. A path on 5 vertices has 4 edges in a line, so at most 2 disjoint edges fit, and edges 1 and 3 or 1 and 4 or 2 and 4 achieve 2.

sourceLine: Matchings, maximal versus maximum, Berge's augmenting-path criterion and Hall's complete-matching condition: GATE Overflow GO Classroom deck (English, read in part) for the matching vocabulary; CLRS ch. 26 for augmenting paths. Standard references used to verify, never copied: Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, ch. 10; West, Introduction to Graph Theory (Brooks, Dirac, Koenig, chromatic polynomial); CLRS ch. 22 (articulation points, bridges) and ch. 26 (bipartite matching); Diestel, Graph Theory (Menger). The path counts, the maximal-versus-maximum example and the half-size bound are recomputed in scripts/validate.py, and the augmenting-path flip is the subject of the lesson.
